echoes.note: "if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is gracious" (2:3) closely reworks Psalm 34:8 LXX (33:9), "taste and see that the Lord is good (chrēstos)." The verb 'tasted' plus the divine predicate is a strong verbal borrowing; the wordplay chrēstos/Christos prepares the turn to the living stone. Psalm 34 recurs across 1 Peter (cf. 3:10-12 quoting Ps 34:12-16), raising recurrence and volume.

"long for the pure milk of the Word" (2:2) picks up the 'word' (logos/rhēma) by which the readers were reborn (1:23-25, where Isa 40:6-8 is just quoted); the abiding word of God is the nourishment metaphor here, an echo carried over from the immediately preceding citation.

"Behold, I lay in Zion a chief cornerstone, chosen, and precious: He who believes in him will not be disappointed" (2:6) is a formula-introduced citation ("it is contained in Scripture") of Isaiah 28:16 LXX. Verbatim: tithēmi en Siōn lithon... eklekton entimon, and the believer not being put to shame. The keywords 'chosen/precious' also reach back to v.4-5 ('chosen by God, precious').

"The stone which the builders rejected, has become the chief cornerstone" (2:7) is a verbatim quotation of Psalm 118:22 LXX (117:22). Part of the stacked stone-testimonia catena; the same text is a primary early-Christian Christological proof (cf. Mark 12:10; Acts 4:11). 'Rejected'/'builders' ties to the rejection theme of v.4.

"a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense" (2:8) quotes Isaiah 8:14, lithos proskommatos kai petra skandalou. Third member of the stone catena, applied to the disobedient who stumble at the word; combined here (as in Rom 9:33) with Isa 28:16.

"a royal priesthood... a holy nation" (2:9) draws directly on Exodus 19:6 LXX, basileion hierateuma kai ethnos hagion, the Sinai vocation of Israel now applied to the church. High volume; the priesthood theme also undergirds v.5 ('holy priesthood... spiritual sacrifices').

"a chosen race... a people for God's own possession, that you may proclaim the excellence of him" (2:9) is woven from Isaiah 43:20-21 LXX, 'my chosen race (genos eklekton)... my people whom I preserved to declare my excellencies (aretas).' The distinctive phrase 'proclaim the excellencies/aretas' is verbatim from Isa 43:21 and not from Exod 19, marking this as a separate source fused into the title-collage.

"a people for God's own possession" (2:9) renders laos eis peripoiēsin, echoing the 'peculiar treasure/possession' (laos periousios / segullah) of Exodus 19:5; reinforces the Sinai covenant frame alongside Exod 19:6, and resonant with Mal 3:17 / Isa 43:21.

"who in time past were no people, but now are God's people, who had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy" (2:10) reworks Hosea 2:23 (LXX 2:25), 'I will say to Not-my-people, You are my people' and 'I will have mercy on Not-pitied.' The double not-people/people and not-mercy/mercy antithesis is the signature of Hosea, also taken up in Rom 9:25.

"were no people, but now are God's people" (2:10) also draws on Hosea 1:9-10, the naming of Lo-ammi ('not my people') and the reversal 'you are sons of the living God.' Companion source to Hos 2:23 supplying the 'not a people' title; high recurrence within the Hosea reversal oracle.

"coming to him, a living stone, rejected indeed by men, but chosen by God" (2:4) anticipates and conditions the catena: the 'rejected by men / chosen by God' contrast frames the stone testimonia of vv.6-8 and the figural identification of Christ as the temple cornerstone before any is formally cited.

"chosen by God, precious" (2:4) pre-echoes Isaiah 28:16's eklekton entimon ('chosen and precious'), the very words cited in v.6; Peter introduces the catena's keywords narratively before quoting, a deliberate framing device.

"rejected indeed by men" (2:4) anticipates 'the stone which the builders rejected' of Ps 118:22 (v.7); apodedokimasmenon shares the rejection motif, weaving the psalm into the opening description of Christ as living stone.

"as living stones, are built up as a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices" (2:5) is a typological reading of the Zion-stone oracle: believers become the new temple founded on Christ the cornerstone, a priesthood offering spiritual (not Levitical) sacrifices. The figural new-temple/new-Israel construal organizes the whole pericope.

"For you who believe therefore is the honor" (2:7) plays on Isa 28:16's 'precious/honor' (entimon/timē) as the antithesis to the builders' rejection of Ps 118:22, binding the two quotations into a single believe/disbelieve contrast.

"I beg you as foreigners and pilgrims" (2:11) echoes the sojourner self-designation paroikos kai parepidēmos of Genesis 23:4 LXX (Abraham), also Psalm 39:12 (LXX 38:13). Reinforces the letter's elect-exile theme (1:1, 1:17); the patriarchal alien status is figurally applied to the diaspora church.

"foreigners and pilgrims" (2:11) also recalls Psalm 39:12 (LXX 38:13), 'I am a sojourner (paroikos) with you and a pilgrim (parepidēmos), as all my fathers were' — the precise LXX pairing of both nouns, supplying the alien-on-earth posture.

"they may by your good works... glorify God in the day of visitation" (2:12) uses 'day of visitation' (hēmera episkopēs), the LXX phrase of Isaiah 10:3 ('what will you do in the day of visitation?'); the Gentiles' eventual glorifying of God when God visits frames the eschatological reckoning behind honorable conduct.

"having good behavior among the nations, so in that of which they speak against you" (2:12) inverts Isaiah 52:5 LXX, 'my name is continually blasphemed among the nations (ethnesin)' — where Israel's conduct caused God's name to be reviled, the church's good works among the nations cause it to be glorified.

"glorify God" through the witness of conduct 'among the nations' (2:12) resonates with Ezekiel 36:23, God sanctifying his name profaned among the nations so that the nations know him; a faint thematic parallel to the vindication-of-the-name motif.

"Fear God. Honor the king" (2:17) closely mirrors Proverbs 24:21 LXX, 'Fear God, my son, and the king (phobou ton theon... kai basilea)' — the paired imperatives toward God and king are a near-verbatim wisdom borrowing structuring the closing quatrain.
Submission 'to the king as supreme' and to governors (2:13-14) reflects the wisdom counsel to keep the king's command (Eccl 8:2-5); a faint thematic backdrop to honoring civil authority.

"who did not sin, 'neither was deceit found in his mouth'" (2:22) quotes Isaiah 53:9 LXX, 'he did no lawlessness, nor was deceit (dolos) found in his mouth.' Verbatim citation of the Servant; anchors the Christ-as-suffering-Servant exemplum.

"when he was cursed, didn't curse back. When he suffered, didn't threaten" (2:23) interprets Isaiah 53:7, 'he was afflicted yet opened not his mouth; like a lamb led to slaughter... he opens not his mouth.' The Servant's silent non-retaliation is the model for unjustly suffering servants.

"who his own self bore our sins in his body on the tree" (2:24) draws on Isaiah 53:4 LXX, 'he bears our sins (houtos tas hamartias hēmōn pherei),' fused with 53:12. The vicarious sin-bearing is the theological core of the Servant application.

"bore our sins in his body" (2:24) also reflects Isaiah 53:12, 'he bore the sins of many (autos hamartias pollōn anēnegken)' — the verb anapherō ('bore/bore up') matches 53:12 LXX, making this a distinct source-clause alongside 53:4.
"by whose stripes you were healed" (2:24) is a near-verbatim citation of Isaiah 53:5 LXX, 'by his bruise (tō mōlōpi autou) we were healed.' Distinctive rare word mōlōps marks high volume.

"For you were going astray like sheep; but now have returned" (2:25) reworks Isaiah 53:6 LXX, 'all we like sheep have gone astray (planēthēmen).' The verb 'gone astray' + 'sheep' is verbatim from the Servant song; the 'returned' supplies the gospel reversal.

"returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls" (2:25) draws on the divine-shepherd oracle of Ezekiel 34, where God himself seeks and gathers the scattered sheep; the straying-sheep/returning-to-shepherd movement of Isa 53:6 is completed with Ezekiel's restoring shepherd imagery.
"the Shepherd... of your souls" (2:25) faintly recalls the Lord-as-shepherd of Psalm 23:1; a thematic resonance of God's pastoral care behind the title applied to Christ.

"that we, having died to sins, might live to righteousness" (2:24) resonates with Isaiah 53:11, the Servant who 'makes many righteous (dikaiōsai dikaion)'; the righteousness outcome of sin-bearing parallels the Servant's justifying work.
The pattern of patient unjust suffering held up as example (2:19-21) reflects the despised-and-rejected Servant of Isaiah 53:3, conditioning the whole exemplum before the formal citations begin.
